issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost Community and culture' is not impossible for a combat trauma survivor, but for a 49-year-old married male European city council member it is the least coherent appraisal in this profile and is weakly anchored to the rest of the selected nodes. The rest of the profile centers on bodily danger, touch/startle, fragmented trauma recall, and safety distrust; this item instead implies a culturally/community dislocation theme that is not supported elsewhere in Triggers/Threat/Memory/Maladaptive Strategies.

issues.item: Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
issues.explanation: 'Overwhelming grief on recall' is not inherently inconsistent, but here it is the least coherent memory item relative to the formulation and other selected items. The profile is dominated by fear-based threat, bodily vulnerability, touch alarm, and cognitive disorganization of recall. A grief-dominant recall item without corresponding loss/bereavement appraisals or related strategies makes the memory cluster less internally aligned.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The profile is largely coherent for a middle-aged male combat survivor, but this appraisal is the main mismatch. 'My body has been permanently damaged' implies a salient lasting physical injury. That idea is not supported elsewhere in the selected profile: memory items focus on fragmented, terror-laden recall; threat items emphasize current danger, mistrust of safety, startle to touch, and sleep disturbance; maladaptive strategies emphasize sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch. There are no triggers selected, and no other items indicate ongoing medical consequences or trauma themes centered on bodily injury. In this profile, the appraisal reads as if it belongs to a different subtype centered on physical injury rather than the represented combat-related fear/terror formulation.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a combat trauma profile in a 49-year-old male, this specific self-blame item is the main coherence problem. The rest of the profile centers on persistent danger, touch-triggered alarm, fragmented/terror-laden memory, and defensive avoidance, which fits combat-related PTSD. In contrast, 'the event happened because of the way I acted' implies a strong internal-causal guilt formulation that is not otherwise supported by the selected memory, threat, or strategy items. This makes the appraisal set less coherent with the overall profile and with the formulation, where Memory and Threat strongly feed Negative Appraisals focused on ongoing danger rather than responsibility for causing the trauma. Self-blame can occur in combat PTSD, but here it is insufficiently connected to the other selected items and stands out as the least clinically coherent item.

vignette: John, a 49-year-old European-American man and married City Council Member, has been experiencing persistent difficulties since his return from combat. His trauma left him with a fragmented sense of self and a pervasive feeling that the world is a dangerous place. John's memories of the traumatic event remain incomplete, making it difficult for him to piece together what happened during those critical moments. When he attempts to recount his experiences, he often loses track of his thoughts and struggles to provide a coherent narrative. The day the trauma occurred was vividly etched in John's memory but with gaps that left him feeling uncertain about many aspects of the event. The chaos and violence were overwhelming; bullets whizzed past him, explosions echoed through the air, and the fear of being hit at any moment kept his senses on high alert. Despite surviving, he carries a deep-seated belief that his body continues to react as if it is still in danger, no matter how safe he truly is. John's hypervigilance has become an integral part of his daily life. He constantly monitors his surroundings and remains on guard at all times, convinced that another threat could arise unexpectedly. This constant state of alertness has taken a toll on his ability to relax or engage in leisure activities without feeling anxious. Even the simplest things, like sitting in his office at City Hall or attending council meetings, can trigger intense feelings of unease. John's hyperarousal manifests in other ways as well. He struggles with sleep problems, finding it difficult to fall asleep and often wakes up several times during the night, each time feeling a surge of anxiety that he must push through until dawn. This lack of rest only exacerbates his hypervigilance and leaves him exhausted. His avoidance behaviors have grown more pronounced over time. Any form of physical contact with others is particularly distressing for John. When someone touches him unexpectedly, such as a handshake from a colleague or an affectionate pat on the back from his wife, he reacts with alarm, his body tensing up instantly and his mind racing to prepare for potential danger. This has created significant strain in both his professional and personal life. In his role at City Hall, John often finds himself avoiding social interactions that might lead to physical contact or close proximity to others. His colleagues have noticed a change in him; he is more distant and less willing to engage in team-building activities or informal gatherings after work. This has affected his ability to collaborate effectively with others and has created some friction within the council. The emotional toll of these symptoms has also taken its toll on John's marriage. He finds it challenging to open up about what he is going through, partly because of his fear that talking about it will make him relive the trauma and partly due to a belief that no one can truly understand or provide comfort. His wife has expressed concern over his increasing isolation and reluctance to seek help. John's maladaptive strategies have only compounded these issues. He often turns to sensory distractions like playing loud music or keeping the TV on to drown out intrusive thoughts, but this has not alleviated his distress. In fact, it has led him to feel more disconnected from others, as he retreats into a world of noise rather than facing his fears. What frightened John most was the feeling that no matter how many times he told himself he was safe, he found it impossible to believe it. The terror on recall of the event was so intense that it overshadowed any attempts at healing or moving forward. He had come to believe that the world would always be a dangerous place and that his body's reactions were a permanent reminder of that fact. Finally, after months of struggling in silence, John decided he could no longer bear the weight of these symptoms alone. The strain on his relationships and his inability to function effectively at work had become too much to handle. He sought help, hoping to regain some semblance of normalcy and find a way to reconcile with his past without it constantly haunting him. John was most afraid that he would never be able to fully trust the safety of his surroundings again. At the same time, he was hopeful that with therapy, he could learn strategies to manage his symptoms and perhaps even begin to rebuild his sense of security in the world around him.
